audit.reasoning: The coding (fixed-dominant penult, not strict) rests on the 2017 LangSci reference grammar, the best and only full description of the language; the deciding sentence is verbatim at sec. 2.2 p. 23, and the stated exceptions (exclamations, dialectal 1sg-length ultima, -chuwan antepenult p. 178) are delimited classes consistent with dominant-not-strict penult. No instrumental or phonology-specific study exists to challenge it. Only housekeeping: the source PDF was not actually in custody (now saved under the audit dir), the locator can be sharpened to 'sec. 2.2, p. 23', and the verify note's '-chuwan p. 177' should read p. 178.

sources.citation: Shimelman 2017, A Grammar of Yauyos Quechua, LangSci SiDL 9, sec. 2.2 full PDF re-read; stated exceptions are exclamations and dialectal ultima stress with 1sg vowel-length marking (delimited, triage-graded penult)
sources.quote: As in the overwhelming majority of Quechuan languages, primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of a word (compare yanápa-n 'he helps' and yanapá-ya-n 'he is helping'; awá-rqa 'he wove' and awa-rqá-ni 'I wove').

sources.citation: Shimelman, Aviva. 2017. A grammar of Yauyos Quechua (Studies in Diversity Linguistics 9). Berlin: Language Science Press. doi:10.5281/zenodo.376355
sources.quote: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of a word (yanápa-n vs yanapá-ya-n; awá-rqa vs awa-rqá-ni); first syllable of words >4 syllables gets weak stress. Exceptions: exclamations often ultima-stressed; in dialects with 1sg vowel length, ultima stress when person marking is word-final (uyari-yá-:); words ending in -chuwan take antepenultimate stress (p. 178).
sources.locator: sec. 2.2, printed p. 23 (PDF p. 43); also sec. 4.3 p. 178 (-chuwan antepenult) and ch. 5 interjections (exclamations final-stressed)
